engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Strategy: Open Files for Rooks
chess.body: Rooks need open files to be active. An open file has no pawns. A semi-open file has only enemy pawns. Double rooks on an open file (called 'Rooks on 7th') is a deadly battery. Strategy: open files by pawn trades, then occupy them immediately. Don't leave your rooks passive on the back rank.

book.author: Simon Sinek
book.chapter: The Golden Circle: Why, How, What
book.lesson: Most companies communicate from the outside in: what they do, then how they do it, then why. Apple communicates from the inside out: why first (we believe in challenging the status quo), then how (by making beautifully designed, simple products), then what (we make computers and phones). The why speaks to the limbic brain — the emotional, decision-making centre. The what speaks to the neocortex — logical but not the driver of decisions. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it. This is why Apple users are more loyal than Dell users, even when specs are comparable.
book.key_quote: People don't buy what you do. They buy why you do it. And they don't care about your what until they believe your why.
book.action: Write your personal WHY in one sentence: 'I exist to _____ so that _____.' Does your daily work reflect this?
crux: The Golden Circle: Why → How → What. Most communicate outside-in; leaders work inside-out.
People don't buy what you do. They buy why you do it.
Why is a belief or purpose. How are the differentiating actions. What are the products.
The Golden Circle maps to biology: What is neocortex (rational), Why is limbic (feeling, trust, loyalty).
That is why 'it feels right' outperforms a superior spec sheet.
Manipulations — price, promotions, fear, novelty — produce transactions, not loyalty.
Clarity, discipline, consistency: know why, hold yourself to how, and be consistent in what.
The Law of Diffusion of Innovation: you need 15–18% adoption before the majority moves.
Sell to the people who believe what you believe first. They are the 2.5% who tolerate imperfection.
Why comes from your past, not from a strategy session. It is discovered.
The Celery Test: given your Why, filtering decisions becomes obvious to observers.
Split of Why happens when the What outgrows the belief. Founders' clarity fades and the company drifts.
Why attracts the right people. Skills can be taught; belief cannot.
learnings: Purpose is a filter, not a slogan. It should visibly kill options.
Trust is limbic. It does not respond to feature lists.
Early believers are worth more than early volume.
If your Why isn't reflected in what you refuse, you don't have one.
examples: Apple sells the same components as Dell but leads with challenging the status quo — and can sell phones and music while Dell could not sell MP3 players.
The Wright brothers beat Samuel Langley, who had funding, Smithsonian backing, and press. They had belief and a team that shared it.
King's 'I have a dream' — not 'I have a plan'. 250,000 arrived without invitations.
adapt: Your Why: most financial advice ignores behaviour, so it fails. That belief explains the content, the products, and the refusals.
The Celery Test kills motivational finance content instantly. It doesn't fit the Why.
Sell Codex to the 2.5% who already believe automation beats hiring. Not to the majority.
Lead the Dubai pitch with the belief, not the CV bullet list. The bullets are the What.

interview_tech.q: Like-for-like sales are +3% but total sales are −2%. What is happening?
interview_tech.a: The existing estate is growing while the total base shrank — you closed stores, or a material store left the LFL set. LFL strips out openings and closures, so the gap is the net space effect. Ask: was the closure deliberate portfolio pruning, in which case −2% total with +3% LFL and better margin is a good outcome; or did leases expire without replacement, which is a pipeline failure. Follow with sales density per sqm — that tells you whether the remaining estate is genuinely stronger.

interview_tech.q: You are consolidating Malaysia and Indonesia. Where do FX translation differences land?
interview_tech.a: Functional currency results are translated at the closing rate for assets and liabilities, average rate for P&L, and the difference goes to other comprehensive income as a foreign currency translation reserve — not through P&L. It only recycles to P&L on disposal of the foreign operation. The trap: intercompany balances that are effectively permanent investment belong in the net investment, so their FX also goes to OCI. Getting that wrong puts noise through earnings every quarter.

interview_soft.q: The board pushes back hard on your numbers in front of everyone. What do you do?
interview_soft.a: Do not defend and do not fold. Separate the challenge into fact and judgement. If they have spotted a factual error, concede immediately and precisely — 'you are right, that is the restated base, I will recirculate by Thursday.' Credibility survives errors; it does not survive defensiveness. If it is a judgement call, state your assumption, the sensitivity, and offer the alternative case. Never argue methodology in the room; take it offline with the one director who raised it.

interview_soft.q: An employee asks you to approve an expense that is within policy but clearly wrong. What now?
interview_soft.a: They are testing whether you hide behind rules. Policy is a floor, not a ceiling. Approve or reject on the substance, explain the reasoning to the person directly, and then fix the policy so the next person is not in the same position. If it involves a senior person, the answer does not change — that is precisely when it counts. Say plainly that you would escalate to the audit committee if pressured to approve something you believe is wrong.
interview_soft.who: Any group with a code of conduct

cfo_field.q: The offer is decided by the non-technical questions.
cfo_field.a: Everyone shortlisted can do the technical work — that is why they were shortlisted. What separates the offer is whether the panel believes you can hold a room, disagree with a CEO without theatre, and be trusted with bad news. Prepare the failure story properly: what you decided, what it cost, what you changed afterwards. A candidate with no failure story reads as someone who has never owned a decision.

cfo_field.q: A forecast that is never wrong is a forecast nobody is using.
cfo_field.a: Track forecast accuracy as a metric in its own right — absolute percentage error by month, by category. Under 5% at group level is good in retail; over 15% and the business has stopped believing you. But an FP&A team that is never wrong is sandbagging, and sandbagging is more expensive than error: it prices in a buffer everyone plans around, and the buffer compounds up the hierarchy.
